If adoption expenses left you with a tax credit you couldn't fully use, the IRS may be sending money back without requiring another round of paperwork. The agency is automatically adjusting certain 2025 tax returns to account for unused adoption credits from earlier years. The change could make more of your credit refundable, subject to a limit of $5,000 per eligible child. Refunds and adjustments began in late September 2026, and the IRS expects most eligible taxpayers to be processed by the end of the year. Families covered by the automatic adjustment generally don't need to file an amended return to receive it. It would be nice to put extra cash in your pocket , but the important questions are whether the IRS has enough information to make the correction and how the adjustment affects your refund and remaining credit. Read More Here › SPONSORED Why the IRS is adjusting refunds The adoption tax credit helps eligible families offset qualified adoption expenses. Previously, it was generally nonrefundable, meaning it could reduce your federal income tax liability but couldn't produce a refund beyond that liability. Beginning with tax year 2025, part of the credit became refundable. Treasury later clarified that, for 2025 only, eligible unused adoption credit carryforwards from 2020 through 2024 can also count toward the refundable portion. That matters for families whose earlier credits went unused because their tax liability was too low. Some of that remaining credit may now generate a refund. The IRS is making these corrections using information already available on taxpayers' returns and accounts. The special treatment of prior-year carryforwards applies only to 2025; families shouldn't assume those carryforwards will be refundable again in 2026. Shopping for cheaper auto insurance? Who could receive an automatic adjustment The automatic process focuses on taxpayers with adoption credit carryforwards available for use in 2025 whose records show they qualify for a larger refundable credit. Taxpayers who filed their 2025 federal return before April 15, 2026, will generally receive any applicable adjustment automatically. Returns filed under an extension and accounts with identity theft indicators, freezes, dependency conflicts, or other unresolved issues may require later review. Those complications don't necessarily mean a family is ineligible. The IRS may need to process the return or resolve the account issue first. You also aren't automatically excluded if you omitted the adoption credit from your 2025 return. The IRS says some taxpayers may still receive an adjustment if a Form 8839 filed for 2020 through 2024 showed an eligible carryforward. However, if the agency lacks enough information to determine your credit, you may need to file an amended return with Form 8839. Why your refund could be less than $5,000 The $5,000 figure is a maximum refundable amount per eligible child for 2025. It isn't a guaranteed payment or an additional $5,000 on top of the refundable adoption credit you already received. Your actual result depends on your allowable credit, available carryforwards, number of eligible children, income limits, other credits, payments, and account balances. An adjustment could produce a smaller refund, reduce an unpaid tax balance, or leave no money to send you. Certain past-due debts could also absorb some or all of a refund. For families with multiple eligible children, the per-child limit may increase the potential refundable amount. Each child's credit must still meet the applicable rules. Qualified adoption expenses generally include reasonable and necessary adoption fees, attorney fees, court costs, and travel expenses directly related to a legal adoption. Expenses reimbursed by an employer or paid by a government program generally don't qualify for the credit. Expenses for adopting your spouse's child are also excluded. A separate rule can help families who finalize an adoption of a qualifying U.S. child with special needs. They may qualify for the full credit even with little or no qualified out-of-pocket expense. For this purpose, "special needs" depends on the required state or Indian tribal government determination. A medical diagnosis alone doesn't establish eligibility under that tax rule. What your IRS notice should explain If the IRS adjusts your account, it will send a notice explaining the change, generally within 30 days of the adjustment. The notice should identify the amount and whether it resulted in a refund or was applied toward another tax or non-tax debt. Compare it with your 2025 return and keep it with your tax records. If you agree with the adjustment, you generally don't need to respond. If something looks wrong, follow the notice's instructions and any response deadline. Keep your Form 8839, adoption expense documentation, employer benefit information, carryforward worksheets, and IRS notice together. If a tax professional prepared your return, share the notice so your records reflect the correction. How to check your adjustment Use your IRS Online Account or request a tax account transcript to look for updated information after processing. The IRS specifically says Where's My Refund? won't show information about this type of adjustment. Checking that tool repeatedly won't help you track this payment. The agency also asks taxpayers not to call solely for an update unless instructed by a notice or letter, because phone representatives don't have additional information beyond the published guidance. An amended return may still be necessary if the IRS lacks required credit information or you need to correct income, filing status, dependents, adoption expenses, employer benefits, or another return item. Before preparing your 2026 return, check your remaining carryforward, too. Credit refunded through the 2025 adjustment may reduce what remains available for future years. Use the corrected carryforward rather than simply copying the amount from your original return. Bottom line Some families with unused adoption credits could receive an automatic refund without filing an amended return. But before you eliminate some money stress , know that the $5,000-per-child limit doesn't guarantee that amount will reach your bank account. Watch for the IRS notice, compare the adjustment with your records, and check your online account if needed. Keeping the corrected credit information together will help you understand this refund and claim the right amount when you file again.
